title: Finding customers for Greptile
lede: Greptile sells an AI code reviewer to engineering teams drowning in agent-written pull requests, and the hard part is that its best-looking prospects are often already running a competitor's bot.

company.name: Greptile
company.one_liner: AI agents that review and test pull requests with context from the whole codebase.

glossary.ICP: Ideal customer profile: the kind of company that buys, and why. It describes a company, not a person.
glossary.persona: One role inside the target company, with what they own and why they would care.
glossary.buying signal: Something you can see from outside that makes the pain urgent now, like a job post or a funding round.
glossary.roll-up: A company that has been bought by a bigger group. The buying decision usually moves to the parent.
glossary.champion: The person inside the account who wants you to win and runs the evaluation for you.
glossary.PR: Pull request: a proposed code change that someone reviews before it is merged.
glossary.DevEx: Developer experience: the team that owns engineers' tools, CI, and increasingly the AI coding and review tools.
glossary.build vs buy: The moment a team decides whether to build a tool in-house or buy one. Greptile's case studies show both Mixpanel and Coinbase tried building first.
glossary.Managed Agent: A Claude agent hosted by Anthropic that runs on a schedule, uses tools, and is graded against a rubric you write.
glossary.rubric: The written definition of done a grader checks each agent run against.
glossary.effort: A setting on current Claude models (low to max) that trades thinking time for cost.

lessons.title: Who buys this?
lessons.idea: The engineer who loves a code reviewer is rarely the one who pays for it. Your {{ICP}} names the company that buys; each {{persona}} names a person inside it.

blocks.name: Positioning against the real alternative
blocks.body: For Greptile the alternative is rarely no tool. It's an in-house review agent or a rival bot already on the pull requests, so position against those.

blocks.heading: Where Greptile's proof clusters
blocks.caption: Greptile's named customers, grouped by this course [s3].

items.label: Company
items.value: Software companies that write their own product code, on GitHub or GitLab [s1]

items.label: Size
items.value: Roughly 150 to 2,000 engineers. The long case studies sit here: Coinbase ~150 engineers, Brex 400+, Scale ~650 [s6, s4, s7]

items.label: Sharpest slice
items.value: Regulated or high-stakes code: fintech, infrastructure, big monorepos [s4, s5]

items.label: Regions
items.value: US first (San Francisco, New York), then English-speaking markets (my judgement, from where the customers and open roles are) [s10]

items.label: The pain, in their words
items.value: "code review is going to be a bottleneck" (Scale) [s7]. "I was drowning in code reviews" (NVIDIA) [s9]. Other tools' feedback "was generic" (Brex) [s4].

items.label: Why now
items.value: Coding agents multiplied {{PR}}s: at Mixpanel, 95% of merged PRs have coding-agent attribution [s5]

items.label: Not a fit
items.value: Existing customers, competitors, a competitor's named customer, companies bought by a bigger group, and teams that already auto-approve PRs with their own reviewer

items.title: VP Engineering or CTO
items.body: Owns headcount and velocity. The quoted buyer at Scale, Datadog and Brex [s7, s8, s4]. Cares because review is now the limit on what agents can ship.

items.title: Head of DevEx or AI Dev Tools
items.body: Your likely {{champion}}. Owns review tooling and often the vendor contract [s22]. At Mixpanel, the platform engineering manager ran the shootout [s5].

items.title: Staff and principal engineers
items.body: The humans doing the reviews. They feel the pain first and will kill a noisy bot fast: Scale's first feedback was "this is annoying" [s7].

items.title: Security or AppSec lead
items.body: Asks where the code goes. Self-hosting, SOC 2 and SSO answer them [s1, s2]. Coinbase runs Greptile next to its own security agents [s6].

blocks.title: The decision, and why
blocks.body:
I looked at three segments. Small startups get a free tier and 50% off, so self-serve covers them [s2]. Air-gapped defense and healthcare fit the self-host story but have no named case study yet [s1].

I picked mid-market and enterprise software teams, because every long case study is one and Greptile is hiring Enterprise and Mid-market AEs right now [s3, s11, s10].

quiz.q: Gusto's staff engineers love a Greptile trial. Who most likely signs a company-wide contract?
options: A staff engineer on the trial
The manager of AI Dev Tools
quiz.why: The DevEx or AI Dev Tools manager runs the evaluation and the paperwork, but the case studies quote VP Engineering and CTOs as the buyer. Win the champion, then get to the signer.

lessons.title: Where are they?
lessons.idea: A target list is only useful if every row is the right company. For Greptile, 12 of the 26 companies I started with failed a check.

blocks.name: Tier your accounts
blocks.body: Almost half the candidates failed a check, most because a rival was already there. The ones left get tiered by timing: a live hiring post or funding round goes first.

blocks.caption: "Clean PRs" means no CodeRabbit, Graphite or Greptile bot commenting on the company's public pull requests in 2026. Checked 2026-09-24.

blocks.title: Two companies called Zip
blocks.body: The procurement company Zip moved from ziphq.com to zip.com. zip.co is Zip Co, a pay-later company [s38, s42]. Both sound like fintech, so only the domain plus what they sell settles it.

blocks.title: The competitor is already in their PRs
blocks.body: Supabase looked great until I searched its public pull requests: CodeRabbit commented on 2,067 of them since August 1 [s20]. That is a displacement sale, not a first sale, so it came off the list.

blocks.title: The perfect signal on the wrong account
blocks.body: Asana posted two Developer Productivity roles on September 17 for its 500+ developers [s39]. But Graphite's homepage features an Asana case study, and Ramp's too [s15]. Great signal, competitor's customer.

blocks.title: Bought by someone bigger
blocks.body: Confluent has been an IBM subsidiary since March 17, a {{roll-up}}: the decision now runs through IBM [s18]. Your own flagship customer can move too: Brex, the first case study on Greptile's homepage, now belongs to Capital One [s19, s4].

blocks.title: They sell it, or they built it
blocks.body: Sentry sells its own AI code review at $40 per contributor [s17]. Intercom built its own reviewer and auto-approves over 19% of PRs with it [s21]. Neither is a buyer this quarter.

blocks.heading: Run these on your own list, in order
items: Open the domain. Name, product and location match what you wrote.
Generic name? Confirm with domain plus what they sell (Zip vs Zip Co).
Search "<company> acquired" and read the newest news first.
Compare against Greptile's customers page, including the logo strip.
Compare against competitors and their customer pages: CodeRabbit [s12, s13], Graphite, now owned by Cursor [s14, s15], Sentry [s17], and Anthropic's own Code Review [s16].
Search the company's public GitHub PRs for a competitor's review bot.
Check fit on the facts: engineering size from their own jobs page or posts.
Can't settle a check? Drop the row. Grafana Labs and Faire came off for this reason.

quiz.q: Your list has "Zip" twice: ziphq.com and zip.co. Which check tells you which one to keep?
quiz.why: ziphq.com redirects to zip.com, a procurement platform; zip.co is a pay-later company. Only the domain and the product tell them apart.

quiz.q: Asana is hiring Developer Productivity engineers this week. Why is it off the list?
options: Graphite publishes an Asana case study
quiz.why: A named customer of a direct competitor is a displacement sale. Keep it on a separate watch list, not in your first 14.

lessons.title: When are they ready?
lessons.idea: The same account is a bad target in March and a great one in September. A {{buying signal}} is something you can see from outside that makes review pain urgent now.

blocks.body: A developer-productivity hiring post is live for about a month; a funding round opens roughly a 90-day window. Mercury's round is 127 days old, so it no longer counts.

blocks.title: Signals go stale
blocks.body: Mercury's $200M round was on May 20, which is 127 days ago and past a 90-day window [s26]. Its July DevEx role is the fresher reason to write [s28]. Job posts matter while they are live; funding for about 90 days.

You don't have to re-run this by hand. In Otto, each of these maps to a Signal Agent that watches the account list and tells you when one fires. Lesson 7 builds a version of the same watch with Claude.

quiz.q: Which of these is a buying signal for Greptile this week?
options: Temporal raised $550M on September 14 and doubled its team
Duolingo is hiring a Senior EM for its AI Platform team
quiz.why: Duolingo's AI Platform team builds AI for the product, not tools for engineers [s37], so it is just news. Mercury's round is past 90 days. Temporal's is ten days old and comes with a team that doubled.

lessons.title: Who exactly?
lessons.idea: Reach the person who owns the review problem, then the person who signs. People change jobs all the time, so check they still work there before you write.

blocks.name: Multi-thread every account
blocks.body: Reach the developer-experience lead who owns the tooling and the VP Engineering who signs. A single contact is one resignation away from a dead deal.

blocks.heading: Roles to reach at each account
rows: Head of DevEx, Developer Productivity or AI Dev Tools
Making agent-written code safe to merge; the vendor shortlist
The hiring manager on the job post (Gusto, Samsara, Instacart [s22, s24, s23]); engineering blog authors
Company leadership page, conference talks, funding press releases
Staff or principal engineer on the platform team
Noise. Will the bot waste their time?
Commit history and PR reviews in public repos; tech talks
Security pages, trust centers, security job posts

blocks.heading: Check a person still works there
items: Their own profile shows the account as current employer, and the company page it links to has the same domain (gusto.com, not a lookalike).
They posted, spoke or committed code for that company in the last 90 days.
The company's own site, blog or job post names them or their team.
Two of three agree? Write. Only one? Keep looking.

blocks.body: This course names roles, not people, because the file may be shared. When you want verified names at each account, Otto can find people by role inside a company and check their current employer against the domain.

blocks.title: Find Gusto's champion
blocks.body:
Open the Gusto AI Tools job post [s22] and note which team it sits in. Find who leads that team and check they still work at gusto.com using the three steps above.

Then find the engineering leader they report to. That is your signer.

lessons.title: What do you say?
lessons.idea: The first message is about them, not you. It proves you looked, makes one point, and asks one easy question.

blocks.name: One ask per message
blocks.body: Ask one question an engineering leader can answer in a line. Two asks get zero answers.

left.label: The message everyone sends
left.body:
Hi {first name}, hope you're well! I'm reaching out from Greptile, the AI code reviewer that helps teams merge 4X faster and catch 3X more bugs. We work with NVIDIA, Brex and Coinbase.

Would you be open to a quick 15-minute call next week to see how we could supercharge your code review?

right.label: Yours, to Gusto
right.body:
Hi {first name}, saw Gusto is hiring a manager for AI Dev Tools, and the post puts automated AI code review and the vendor contracts in the same job.

That usually means agent-written PRs are arriving faster than reviewers can read them, and someone has to decide build or buy.

Are you leaning toward building the reviewer in-house, or running a bake-off first?

(Mixpanel ran that bake-off, in-house build included, before picking Greptile.)
right.notes: Opens on their job post [s22], not on us. Names the pain as they would. One either/or question they can answer from memory. The last line is a fact from a case study [s5], not a claim about results. No meeting ask. 71 words.

items.title: Open on them
items.body: Their signal, in their words: "automated AI code review" and "vendor contracts" are straight from the post.

items.title: One point
items.body: Build or buy is the decision this hire exists to make. Nothing about benchmarks.

items.title: One easy question
items.body: Either/or, answerable in five words. No calendar link.

items.title: Under 90 words
items.body: No em dashes, no exclamation marks, no "hope you're well".

blocks.title: Know who else is in the room
blocks.body: Cursor's agent already works on PRs in one of Gusto's public repos [s40], and Cursor also sells a reviewer. Don't mention it in message one. Do expect Bugbot in the bake-off.

quiz.q: Which opening line gets a reply?
options: Hope you're well! Greptile helps teams merge 4X faster.
I'm the founder of Greptile and we just raised from Benchmark.
Saw your AI Dev Tools post puts AI code review and vendor contracts in one job.
quiz.why: The first is about the product, the second is about you. The third proves you read their post and sets up one question.

lessons.title: Which model for which job?
lessons.idea: Bulk sorting doesn't need the biggest model; judgement calls do. So I ran one real task from this course on three Claude models and measured it.

blocks.name: Match the tool to the job
blocks.body: Use the smallest model that sorts accounts well at volume, and the biggest where a mistake is expensive. Decide by measurement, like this.

blocks.takeaway: On a sorting task with written rules, Haiku got 14 of 15 for about a ninth of Opus's cost and in a third of the time. Its miss was a careless read (acquirer vs acquired) and it padded two reasons with facts that were not on the page, so use it for volume and spot-check its reasons. Sonnet and Opus were both perfect; Opus was faster than Sonnet here and flagged its own gaps, which is what you want on the calls that matter.

rows: Sorting hundreds of accounts, pulling fields from job posts

Researching an account, drafting messages at volume
15/15 with reasons that stayed close to the facts
The ICP decision, a message to a key account like Gusto, grading the scheduled agent
15/15 and the only one that said what it didn't know. $0.033 for this run

blocks.body: Every current model also takes an {{effort}} setting, from low to max. A bigger model on lower effort is sometimes a better trade than a smaller model.

quiz.why: Haiku got 14 of 15 at about a ninth of Opus's cost. Its miss and its two invented details are exactly why you check a sample of reasons, not just labels.

lessons.title: Can this run without me?
lessons.idea: Everything in lessons 2 to 5 can run every week without you. A {{Managed Agent}} is a model with instructions, tools and a {{rubric}} it is graded against.

blocks.title: Cost and control
blocks.body:
Each run's cost shows in the Claude Console, and `RUN_BUDGET_CENTS` in `.env` is a hard cap per run (500 means $5). I didn't run the agent, so there is no measured cost to quote. The lab suggests Sonnet is enough for weekly research: set `MODEL=claude-sonnet-5` before launching to spend less.

The agent only writes a report. It doesn't email, post or change anything.

quiz.q: The first run flags a company that was acquired last month. What do you change so it doesn't happen again?
quiz.why: Who to skip belongs in the brief the agent works from. Add a rubric line too if it keeps slipping through, so the grader sends the run back.

blocks.heading: Setting up a campaign in Otto from this course
items: Import the lesson 2 table into a workbook named after the course, with each domain, so Otto matches existing companies (`import_leads`).
Add the people you found for each persona as a dry run first (`import_people`). Every person should attach to an imported company, with no new companies created.
Pick a template and create a draft campaign (`list_templates`, `campaign_from_template`). Nothing launches.
Put the Gusto-style message in as step 1, plus one or two follow-ups that bring a different finding, not the same pitch (`edit_campaign_sequence`).
Enrol the workbook and set send days, window, time zone and a daily cap (`add_to_campaign`, `update_campaign`).
Run the pre-launch check (`campaign_setup_review`). It lists what's missing: leads, copy, a connected mailbox or LinkedIn account, a schedule.
Launch it yourself when you've read the copy. Replies land in Otto's inbox.

blocks.title: Nothing sends until you launch it
blocks.body: Otto wasn't connected for this run, so no draft campaign exists. Start at [otto-pilot.io](https://otto-pilot.io) when you're ready.

quiz.q: The pre-launch check says "no mailbox that can see replies". What happens if you try to launch anyway?
options: It sends and you miss the replies
Otto refuses to launch until the blocker is fixed
It sends from a default address
quiz.why: Blockers in the pre-launch check stop the launch. Connect the mailbox, re-run the check, then launch.
